title: The Buddha lets the breath be
hookLine: the second visit: a man who once tried to stop his breath, and learned to simply know it
carry: anapanasati: know the breath, don't steer it
last: SEVA — EVERYONE AT THE SAME HEIGHT.

lines: HE TRIED TO STOP HIS BREATH.
cards: Before he was the Buddha, he was a prince who left everything to find the end of suffering. For years he pushed his body as hard as a body can be pushed. In the old Pali texts he tells it himself.
He tried stopping his breath, through mouth and nose, until his head pounded as if it were being split. He ate so little that, touching his belly, he could feel his spine. None of it worked.
And then, he says, he remembered a day from his childhood: sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father worked, calm and happy, without trying at all. Could that be the way?

teach.h: HE ATE AGAIN. HIS FRIENDS LEFT.
teach.b: So he ate again, and his five companions walked off, sure he'd given up. He hadn't. He sat down and turned to the breath, not to force it but to know it.
Elsewhere he says that before his awakening, this was how he mostly dwelt.

The practice Buddhists keep from his teaching is called anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, and a discourse of that name lays it out almost like stage directions. Go to the forest, the root of a tree, an empty hut.
Mindful, breathe out. Breathing in long, know: I breathe in long. Breathing in short, know: I breathe in short.
That's the first surprise: nothing is being fixed. Many teachers point out the turn: the man who once tried to stop his breath now simply knows it. The second surprise is how far it goes.
The discourse lays out sixteen steps, from the length of the breath, through the body calming, then feelings, then the mind itself, to watching everything change and letting go. And why the breath?
Because it's always here, and it never stays. Buddhists call that anicca, impermanence, and the breath teaches it every few seconds. Now, from your own door.
You may know pranayama from a yoga class: an old Hindu practice where the breath is counted, held and lengthened on purpose.
That's a real path, and it's a different one. In the Buddha's hall, you don't steer the breath. You know it.

how: Many Buddhists, in Theravada, Zen and Tibetan communities alike, practice mindfulness of breathing, sitting quietly and knowing each breath as it comes and goes, often in a hall with a bell to begin and end.

o: holding the breath to build up inner power
knowing each breath as it comes, without steering it
slow, counted breathing to calm the body down

games.q: inside the Buddhist breath — tap the pairs.
p: mindfulness of breathing in and out
a calm he remembered from childhood
from the breath to letting go

s: Buddhist breath meditation means controlling the breath
the sutta's instruction is to know the breath, long or short, not to steer it.
the Anapanasati Sutta lays out sixteen steps
from the length of the breath, through body, feelings and mind, to letting go.
the Buddha found his way by holding his breath longer than anyone
he tried stopping his breath, and it only brought pain. he turned to knowing the breath instead.

games.q: you're in the hall. your breath is short and shallow. what does the sutta tell you to do?
o: take a slow deep breath to fix it.
know it: I breathe in short.
count to four on each breath.
games.why: breathing in short, he knows: I breathe in short. nothing is fixed. the practice is knowing.

practice: Sit, back straight, the way the text describes, and don't change the breath: when it comes in long, know it's long; when it comes in short, know it's short.
When your mind wanders off, and it will, notice that too, and come back to the next breath. No counting, no holding, no goal: just a guest sitting quietly in someone else's hall.

wordCard.voice: Anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing in and out. Not steering it; knowing it, and watching it change.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: ana and apana, the breath in and out, + sati, mindfulness.

carryVoice: Your line: anapanasati, know the breath, don't steer it. See you at the third house tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 36 (the breathless meditations and the austerities; the memory of the rose-apple tree; taking food again; the five companions leave)
Anapanasati Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 118 (sixteen steps; fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness)
Padipopama Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 54.8 (before his awakening, the Buddha generally dwelt in concentration by mindfulness of breathing)
Mahasatipatthana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 22 (the breathing instructions: long, short, knowing)
Yoga Sutra 2.49 (pranayama: regulating the flow of the breath)
